entry.title: Mine is worth more.
entry.dek: Same mug, same choice between the mug and the money: the students holding it asked $7.12, the ones who were not asked $3.12. Owning it for one experiment was worth $4.00.
body: “Nothing changes about a thing the moment it becomes mine. Only the price I ask for it.”

Have you ever asked yourself why the things you own always seem to be worth more than anybody is willing to pay for them? Today is Tuesday, the 24th of November, Black Friday is in three days, and this week everybody I know is doing the same thing: trying to sell something old so they can buy something new. The old headphones, the jacket worn twice, the console from two generations ago. And almost everybody is surprised by the same thing - nobody wants to pay what we think our stuff is worth. So the question is: is everybody else wrong, or are we? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at has a name in psychology, the endowment effect, and the short version is: the moment something becomes yours, it becomes more valuable to you. Not because it changed. Because you own it. I met it in my own week before I knew its name, every time I put a price on something old and then got annoyed that nobody agreed with it. Housel says something close to this in “The Psychology of Money” - people do not behave like spreadsheets - and this is one of the clearest examples of it I have found.

Firstly, let’s split the title in two, the way I like to do. “Mine” and “worth more”. The first word is the whole trick. When I look at a thing in a shop, I ask “what do I get if I buy it?”. When I look at the same thing in my room, I ask “what do I lose if I sell it?”. It is the same object, but the question is turned upside down, and losing something feels worse than getting it feels good. Two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, even put a number on that in 1992: in their data, a loss weighed about 2.25 times as much as a gain of the same size. Selling is not a trade in my head, it is a small loss, and I charge for it.

Secondly, let’s look at the experiment that made this famous, because the numbers surprised me. In 1990, Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler published a set of experiments with the most boring object possible: a coffee mug with a university logo. In one of them, the students were split into three groups. The sellers got a mug and were asked at what price they would sell it. The buyers got nothing and were asked how much they would pay for one. And the choosers also got nothing, but for every price they could pick: the mug or the money. Here are the median answers:
Sellers: $7.12
Choosers: $3.12
Buyers: $2.87

Now look closely at the sellers and the choosers, because this is the part I could not stop thinking about. They had exactly the same decision in front of them - at the end, you leave with a mug or you leave with money. The only difference is that for the sellers, the mug was already in their hands. And that difference was worth:
$7.12 - $3.12 = $4.00
$7.12 ÷ $2.87 = 2.48 times what the buyers would pay
Four dollars, for a mug that they had owned only since the start of the session (yes, you read that right, not days, not weeks). Owning something for one experiment was enough to more than double its price.

And when I think about it, the mug is the easy case. Let’s take an old phone as the example. It has two years of photos on it, the scratch from the day it fell, the messages from the summer. A buyer sees a used phone with a scratch. The owner sees a used phone with a scratch plus a story, and wants to be paid for the story. The problem is that the story does not leave with the phone. The buyer gets only the phone. So when we put the price on it, we are charging somebody for something they will never receive.

Thirdly, the place where this stops being funny is money. In my review of “The Psychology of Money” I wrote that most people do not fail because they are not smart, but because they are not emotionally stable when the market goes down. There is a study on that too, by Terrance Odean, from 1998, with a very honest title: “Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?”. He looked at the trades of thousands of ordinary investors and found that they sold their winning stocks much more readily than their losing ones. It is the same mug, only more expensive - the losing stock is mine, selling it would make the loss real, so I keep it and wait for it to “come back”. Holding on feels like patience, but sometimes it is just the endowment effect with a bigger bill.

So here is the test I am going to use this week, before I sell anything and especially before I keep anything. For every object, subscription or project I am holding on to, I ask one question: “If I did not have this, would I buy it today, at this price?”. It is the choosers’ question from the experiment - not “what do I lose?”, but “mug or money?”. If the answer is no, then I am not keeping it because it is worth it. I am keeping it because it is mine.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think the endowment effect explains half of the things in my room and at least one of my projects, and the $4.00 gap is the most useful number I have found this month. But I have to be honest about two things. First, the effect is not as solid as the famous version makes it sound - in 2005, Charles Plott and Kathryn Zeiler ran the mug experiment again with very careful instructions and the gap mostly disappeared, so part of it may be about how the question is asked, not only about ownership. And second, some things really are worth more to me than to anybody else, and that is not a mistake. A watch from a grandfather is not overpriced, it is just not for sale. The trick is to know which things are which, and to be honest that most of my stuff is not the watch.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“Nothing changes about a thing the moment it becomes mine. Only the price I ask for it.”
